tagline.text: A Spanish-era belfry in Laoag said to sink a little more every year

location.label: Location
location.text: Corner of Paco Roman Street and A. Bonifacio Street, Barangay 14, Laoag City, Ilocos Norte

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0–500 (per person; free tower viewing, local transport and snacks)

children.text: The Laoag Sinking Bell Tower is a Spanish-era brick belfry about

tall in the middle of downtown Laoag. It earned the name "Sinking Bell Tower" from the story that its weight is slowly pushing it into the sandy ground, and it still rings the bells of St. William's Cathedral, making it the center of a stroll through the city.

The Laoag Sinking Bell Tower is an old belfry in Laoag, the capital of Ilocos Norte in the northwest of the Philippines. It serves St. William's Cathedral (Laoag Cathedral) but stands apart from the church building rather than attached to it. The distance to the church is reported as about
(about 280 feet), so you can walk it in a minute. The tower is said to be about

tall and was once described as one of the tallest bell towers in the Philippines. Four tiers support a double dome topped with a cross, and the tower is described as holding six bells. Stories say the high-pitched ringing from the third tier could be heard in neighboring towns.

The name comes from the idea that the tower is sinking. A heavy brick tower stands on weak, sandy ground, and it is commonly said to settle about 1 inch (about 2.5 cm) into the earth every year. Unlike the Leaning Tower of Pisa, it is said to sink almost straight down, which is part of its charm. Note, however, that this figure is a "commonly told story" repeated by travel blogs and Wikipedia, not a value confirmed by structural monitoring. The story often comes with another detail: the entrance was once tall enough for a person on horseback, but today you have to stoop to get in, and this is the evidence most often cited that the tower has sunk. Either way, the story has made it the first place many first-time visitors to Laoag photograph.
Sources disagree on when it was built. Many travel guides and blogs say Augustinian friars built it in

during the Spanish era, while English Wikipedia says, a little more cautiously, that it appears to have been built after the 1707 earthquake. For that reason this guide does not pin down an exact year and simply calls it an old brick belfry from the Spanish colonial period. One thing is clear: the tower has survived several minor earthquakes, which is why scholars call the style "Earthquake Baroque." The thick corner columns, the winding stairway inside and the brick laid with lime and sand show how buildings were made in earthquake-prone Philippines. A large clock reportedly once hung on the west face. The "sinking tower" even appears on Laoag's city seal, which shows how much it is treated as a symbol of the city.

The Laoag Sinking Bell Tower is on the Philippines' list of national cultural properties. English Wikipedia's list of cultural properties in the Ilocos Region gives its address as "Paco Roman corner A. Bonifacio Street, Brgy. 14." The same list includes about twenty properties in downtown Laoag alone, including the cathedral, city hall, the Rizal monument and the Museo Ilocos Norte, so the tower makes a good starting point for walking through the old town. The tower itself takes only
5–10 minutes

to see, so this guide is not about making a long trip for the tower alone. It explains how to use the tower as the first stop on a half-day stroll through Laoag and an Ilocos Norte trip. Because Laoag is far from Manila, most travelers fly in or take an overnight bus and combine the tower with other sights.

blocks.title: A four-tier brick tower with a sinking story

children.text: A double dome and a cross sit on top of a four-tier structure about

high. Up close, the grain of the bricks and the thick walls show why it was called a "famously sturdy old tower." The view from the road is good, but walking around the corner and looking from several angles makes it look more three-dimensional.

The doorway at the base is now so low that you have to stoop to pass through. Stories say that long ago a person could ride in on horseback, and the explanation that the ground level rose as the tower went down comes from here. However, the general public is reportedly not allowed inside, so enjoy it by taking a comparison photo at the door.

As the view that dates it after the 1707 earthquake suggests, Spanish-era church architecture in the Philippines was built thick and sturdy to withstand quakes. The heavy corner columns and the winding stairway are typical features. Compare it with Paoay Church in the Ilocos region and you can read the same architectural sense.
The cathedral, just
1–2 minutes
on foot from the tower, stands out for its Italian Renaissance-style facade and capiz-shell windows. It became a cathedral in
when the Diocese of Laoag was established, and Mass is still held on Sundays and holy days. Dress with your shoulders and knees covered.

This tower is not a ruin but a working belfry. Its bells reportedly call people to Mass at the cathedral and ring out over the town, so you may hear them if the timing is right. The ringing times change with the daily Mass schedule, so check locally.

blocks.title: A walk through Laoag's heritage buildings

children.text: English Wikipedia's list of cultural properties in the Ilocos Region also includes Laoag City Hall, the Rizal monument, the Museo Ilocos Norte and the Ligot House. They are all in the city center, so after seeing the tower you can stroll slowly and add one or two of them to fill the day.

blocks.title: Good photos by day and at dusk

children.text: By day the brick color stands out, and at sunset the tower makes a silhouette against the sky. One blogger wrote that it was pleasant to stop by at night, eat street food and stroll. It is in the middle of downtown with plenty of traffic, so watch the roadside when you take photos.

blocks.title: The welcome sign and downtown atmosphere

children.text: Markets, city hall, fast-food shops and supermarkets surround the tower, so the area feels more like a working city than a tourist site. Many travelers also take souvenir photos in front of the big "LAOAG" welcome sign somewhere in town. It is also convenient for buying supplies or finding a place to change money.

items.title: Half-day downtown stroll
items.subtitle: Bell tower, cathedral and old town

children.text: Eat breakfast at your hotel and head to the tower in the city center. Photograph the doorway and the brick texture early, when few people are around.
Walk to St. William's Cathedral and look at the facade and interior. Keep quiet during Mass.
Walk around the plaza near city hall and the Rizal monument and find one or two buildings from the cultural properties list.
If the Museo Ilocos Norte is open, look at the local history and everyday artifacts. Check opening hours and the entrance fee locally.
Eat lunch at a restaurant near the market and try Ilocano food.
Rest at your hotel to avoid the heat, or move on to your next destination.
The tower itself takes only
5–10 minutes
to see. The rest of the time is filled with the cathedral, a walk through town and meals.

items.title: Ilocos Norte day trip
items.subtitle: From Laoag to the northern sights

children.text: Leave your hotel, take a quick look at the tower and cathedral first and take photos.
Rent a vehicle or join a tour and head toward Paoay Church and the La Paz Sand Dunes.
Eat lunch on the way or come back to Laoag for it.
Pick one or two sights on the northern coast, such as the Bangui Windmills or Kapurpurawan Rock.
Return to Laoag for dinner and see the tower once more lit up in the evening.
Travel between sights is about
30 minutes–1.5 hours
by car, depending on traffic. Leave plenty of slack in your schedule.
A nonstop flight from Manila (MNL) to Laoag International Airport (LAO) is reported to take about
1 hour 15 minutes

Cebu Pacific and Philippine Airlines are listed on this route, and some sources say a regional airline subsidiary also flies it. The number of flights varies by season, so check the airlines' official timetables.
From the airport to the city you can take a taxi, a tricycle or a hotel pickup. Check fares locally.
Companies such as Partas, GV Florida, Dominion, Philippine Rabbit and Fariñas are reported to run daily direct buses from Manila to Laoag.
The trip is said to take about
10–12 hours
, so an overnight bus that arrives in the morning is common. The distance between Manila and Laoag is about
490km
(by the southern route, per Wikipedia).
Terminal locations, departure times and fares differ by company, so check each company's notices before you leave.
From Manila, take NLEX, SCTEX and TPLEX, then follow the Ilocos coastal road north. Allow at least half a day of driving, including breaks.
Hiring a car with a driver is also a popular option.
Laoag has taxis, jeepneys, tricycles and kalesa (horse-drawn carriages).
The cathedral, the tower, city hall and the market are all within walking distance of each other.

In Laoag the dry season runs from November to April and the wet season from May to October. Since you see the tower outdoors, the drier months are more comfortable, and December to February in particular tends to be relatively cool and clear, which suits a stroll through the city.
Laoag is described as a region that averages four to five typhoons a year. From July to October flights may be canceled or plans may shift, so leave some slack and check the forecast.

Laoag is the central city of Ilocos Norte, and a range of lodging from budget stays to upscale hotels is reported. Staying near the tower and cathedral makes it easy to walk around town, and a place near the airport is handy for an early flight. Book early in peak season and over holiday weekends.

Ilocano food is one of the joys of traveling here. Well-known local dishes include the Ilocos empanada (a fried snack of rice-flour dough filled with vegetables, egg and sausage), bagnet (crispy fried pork), pinakbet (a vegetable stew) and longganisa, the Ilocano sausage. You can eat them at local markets and on the street, and prices differ by vendor, so ask before you order.
The tower takes only 5 to 10 minutes to see, so plan a half-day that combines it with the cathedral, a walk through town and a meal.
The general public is reportedly not allowed inside the tower. Enjoy it by taking photos at the door.
A photo of a person standing in front of the low doorway makes it easy to compare how far the tower has sunk.
When entering the cathedral, wear clothing that covers your shoulders and knees.
To avoid the midday heat, go early in the morning or around sunset.
Northern Ilocos is not easy to get around, so renting a vehicle or joining a tour is more efficient.
If you plan to combine Laoag with Paoay, Bangui and Pagudpud, use Laoag as your base and stay a night or two.
Opening hours and access can change, so check the latest notices and local conditions.
Access by the general public is reportedly restricted for structural safety reasons. Do not enter or climb the tower without permission.
The "sinks 1 inch a year" figure is a commonly told story, not a value confirmed by structural monitoring. For safety, do not get too close or touch the walls.
The construction date is disputed between the 1612 account and the post-1707-earthquake account. Treat any explanation you hear as a reference only.
The narrow streets in the city center have a lot of traffic. Watch the road side when you take photos.
During the July–October typhoon season, flight and bus plans may change.
Travel blog information is often out of date, so check opening hours and fees locally.
An introduction to the city that holds the tower. You can read more about city attractions such as city hall, the museum and the market, as well as transport information, in the Laoag entry.
A World Heritage church about
30 minutes
by car from Laoag. You can compare it with the same kind of Earthquake Baroque architecture, known for its thick buttresses.
Desert-like sand dunes on the northwestern coast of Laoag, popular for 4x4 rides and sandboarding. Going in the late afternoon gives you beautiful sunsets.
A row of giant wind turbines along the northern coast. It is about
1.5 hours
by car from Laoag, and it fits well into a day trip.
A Spanish-era old city in Ilocos Sur to the south, famous for its stone houses and cobblestone streets. It is about
2 hours
by car from Laoag.
